summary: The seventh day completes the creation sequence as God rests and makes it holy. A new “generations” heading narrows the account to a man formed from dust, a planted garden with a food boundary, and a woman made as a comparable partner.
whyItMatters: The chapter connects created life with rest, work, limits, and companionship. Its garden scene sets the specific command and relationships tested in chapter 3.

context.author: Genesis names no historical writer. Jewish and Christian tradition associates the Torah with Moses; the book briefing describes older traditions shaped into a final literary form, without a settled account of every stage.
context.audience: The book addresses Israel through a story of shared human origins and the family from whom Israel traces its ancestry; no single first audience is named in this chapter.
context.date: The narrated events belong to primeval or ancestral time, not to a securely dated writing event. Major stages of Genesis are often placed across the monarchic to Persian periods, with exact models and dates debated.
context.setting: The seventh day and the garden eastward in Eden, with a river and named branches.
context.literaryForm: Creation conclusion followed by a focused garden narrative, naming scene, and explanation of union.

before.text: Chapter 1 ends with the sixth day and God’s verdict that everything made is very good. The seventh day is the unfinished part of that sequence.

here.text: The chapter moves from holy rest into a focused garden account: a human is formed, placed and commanded, then given a comparable partner.

after.text: The serpent challenges the garden food boundary, and the man and woman eat from the forbidden tree.

outline.heading: Seventh day blessed
outline.note: God finishes, rests, blesses, and sanctifies the seventh day.

outline.heading: Generations and a human from dust
outline.note: The focus shifts to ground without a tiller and a living human formed by God.

outline.heading: Garden, trees, and rivers
outline.note: Eden contains nourishing trees, two named central trees, and a branching river.

outline.heading: Cultivation and food boundary
outline.note: The man is placed to cultivate and keep, with broad permission and one prohibition.

outline.heading: Animals and the search for a partner
outline.note: God says solitude is not good; naming animals does not supply a comparable helper.

outline.heading: Woman, kinship, and union
outline.note: A woman is made and welcomed, and the pair are described as one flesh and unashamed.

keyVerses.text: God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy, because he rested in it from all his work of creation which he had done.
keyVerses.why: The blessed seventh day completes the opening creation sequence.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.
keyVerses.why: The human is placed in the garden with a task before the prohibition is given.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.”
keyVerses.why: “Not good” introduces the need for companionship within a previously good world.

questions.question: Where does the seventh day belong?
questions.answer: The first three verses finish the six-day sequence of chapter 1: God rests from completed work and blesses the seventh day. The new “generations” heading in verse 4 then begins a more focused account of earth and human life.

questions.question: What is a “living soul” here?
questions.answer: The phrase describes the man after God forms him from dust and breathes life into him. The verse portrays the living person as a whole; it does not separately define an immortal component.

questions.question: Why is the garden not simply a place of leisure?
questions.answer: The man is put there to cultivate and keep it. Work appears before the disobedience in chapter 3, while the surrounding trees and water make the garden a place of provision.

questions.question: What does “you will surely die” mean when the pair live beyond the next chapter?
questions.answer: The command states death as the consequence of eating, but this chapter does not explain the timing or manner of that death. The following story must be read before resolving the tension; the text does not say that physical death occurs that same instant.

questions.question: What is said about the two special trees?
questions.answer: The tree of life and the tree of knowledge of good and evil are both named in the garden. The command singles out the knowledge tree as forbidden, while the tree of life becomes important again at the end of chapter 3.

questions.question: What does “helper comparable to him” mean in this scene?
questions.answer: God says the man’s solitude is not good, and no animal brought for naming proves a comparable partner. The woman is then presented as his own bone and flesh; the narrative stresses a fitting human counterpart rather than defining her as a servant.

questions.question: Does the account of a woman made from a rib settle every question of status or gender?
questions.answer: The scene identifies a shared human kinship and the man’s delight in meeting her. It gives an origin story for their union but does not set out a full hierarchy of social roles; readers have argued about those implications beyond these verses.

questions.question: Why mention that they were naked and not ashamed?
questions.answer: The closing line describes the pair before the serpent’s encounter and contrasts sharply with their sudden awareness and covering in chapter 3. It sets up the change in their relation to each other and to God.

glossary.def: The named garden region where God places the formed human and provides trees and water.
To work the garden, paired with keeping it as the human task in verse 15.
The comparable partner sought for the man after the animals do not meet that need.
